mcqs.question: Why does BFS require a queue rather than a stack?
options: A queue's FIFO order processes nodes in discovery order, guaranteeing every node at the current level is exhausted before any node at the next level begins
Queues use less memory than stacks in every case
A stack cannot store tree nodes
BFS can use either a queue or a stack interchangeably with identical results
mcqs.explanation: The level-by-level guarantee BFS provides depends entirely on processing nodes in the order they were discovered, which is exactly FIFO behavior — swapping in a stack (LIFO) would process the most recently discovered node next, producing something closer to DFS instead. Memory usage between the two isn't inherently different, stacks can certainly store tree nodes, and the two structures produce genuinely different traversal orders.

mcqs.question: In the zigzag level-order solution, why does the underlying node-discovery order stay left-to-right on every level, even for levels whose output is reversed?
options: Reversing the discovery order itself would break the left/right child relationships needed to correctly enqueue the next level, so only the output presentation is reversed
The discovery order must alternate to match the output direction
Discovery order and output order are unrelated concepts with no connection
Zigzag traversal requires a completely different tree structure
mcqs.explanation: Enqueuing children in a consistent left-to-right order is what keeps the next level's traversal correct; reversing that discovery order would scramble which children get processed when. So only the already-collected level's output list gets reversed for presentation, never the traversal mechanics themselves. Discovery order and output order are related but intentionally decoupled here, and no structural change to the tree is needed.

mcqs.question: Why does BFS have a natural early-exit advantage over DFS when finding the minimum depth to any leaf?
options: DFS cannot visit leaf nodes at all
BFS is always faster than DFS on every tree problem
The first leaf BFS discovers is guaranteed to be at the minimum depth, since BFS never visits a deeper node before exhausting all shallower ones, so it can return immediately
Minimum depth cannot be computed with DFS under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: BFS's level-by-level guarantee means the very first leaf it encounters must be the shallowest one, since nothing deeper is ever explored before shallower nodes are exhausted — allowing an immediate return with no further work. DFS can absolutely find leaves and can solve minimum depth (by tracking the minimum across all paths), it just lacks this early-exit property and may do more work in the worst case; BFS isn't universally faster for every tree problem.

mcqs.question: Why must `level_size = len(queue)` be captured before the inner loop starts, rather than relying on the loop bound to update naturally?
options: Because children get enqueued onto the same queue during the inner loop, so the queue's length changes mid-level and must be snapshotted first to know exactly how many nodes belong to the current level
Because Python requires all loop bounds to be pre-computed constants
It doesn't matter — any way of bounding the inner loop produces the same grouping
Because the queue must be sorted before counting its size
mcqs.explanation: Since processing each node in the current level enqueues its children into the very same queue, the queue's size changes during the inner loop — capturing the count beforehand is what correctly isolates just this level's nodes rather than bleeding into the next level's. This isn't a language syntax requirement in general, the grouping absolutely depends on getting this right, and no sorting is involved.
